prompt_mask:
An aquarium initially holds ${{V}}L$ of water containing ${{q0}}kg$ of dissolved minerals.
A solution containing ${{c}}kg/L$ of dissolved minerals is pumped into the aquarium at a rate of ${{rin}}L/min$, while the completely mixed water is drained out at a rate of ${{rout}}L/min$. If the amount of minerals $Q(t)$, in kilograms, in the tank $t$ minutes after pumping begins is given by
$Q(t) = α(1 - \frac{t}{{{B}}}) + β(1 - \frac{t}{{{B}}})^{3}$
where $α$ and $β$ are constants, what is the value of $α + β$?

> A scientific calculator is required to answer this question.

A storage tank initially holds ${{V}}\,\text{L}$ of liquid containing ${{q0}}\,\text{kg}$ of dissolved stabilizer.
A feed solution containing ${{c}}\,\text{kg/L}$ of the stabilizer is pumped into the tank at a rate of ${{rin}}\,\text{L/min},$ while the completely mixed liquid is drained out at a rate of ${{rout}}\,\text{L/min}.$
Find, rounded to two decimal places, the amount of stabilizer in the tank ${{T}}$ minutes after pumping begins.

A processing tank initially holds ${{V}}\,\text{L}$ of liquid containing ${{q0}}\,\text{kg}$ of dissolved preservative.
A feed solution containing ${{c}}\,\text{kg/L}$ of the preservative is pumped into the tank at a rate of ${{rin}}\,\text{L/min},$ while the completely mixed liquid is drained out at a rate of ${{rout}}\,\text{L/min}.$
Find, rounded to two decimal places, the amount of preservative in the tank ${{T}}$ minutes after pumping begins.
solution_mask:
Let $Q$ be the amount of preservative in the tank at time $t,$ in minutes. Then, the derivative 

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}
$$

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t.$ This is equal to the rate at which preservative enters the tank minus the rate at which preservative leaves the tank.

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}
$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{kg}/\text{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which preservative enters the tank.

Note that a feed solution containing ${{c}}\,\text{kg/L}$ of the preservative enters the tank at a rate of ${{rin}}\,\text{L/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *preservative* enters the tank is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =({{c}}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}})\cdot ({{rin}}\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =({{c}}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\cancel{\text{L}}})\cdot ({{rin}}\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}}) \\  & ={{J}}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which preservative exits the tank.

To find the rate at which preservative leaves the tank, we must first determine the volume of liquid in the tank at time $t.$

The tank initially contains ${{V}}\,\text{L}$ of liquid; a solution enters at ${{rin}}\,\text{L/min}$ and leaves at ${{rout}}\,\text{L/min}.$
As a result, the volume of liquid in the tank after $t$ minutes is 

$$
{{V}}+{{rin}}t-{{rout}}t=({{V}}+{{delta}}t)\,\text{L}.
$$

Since $Q$ is the amount of preservative in the tank, the *concentration* of the mixed solution at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{{{V}}+{{delta}}t}\,\text{kg/L}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed liquid leaves at a rate of ${{rout}}\,\text{L/min},$ *preservative* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =({{rout}}\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{{{V}}+{{delta}}t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}}) \\  & =({{rout}}\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{{{V}}+{{delta}}t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\cancel{\text{L}}}) \\  & =\frac{{{rout}}Q}{{{V}}+{{delta}}t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{2Q}{{{B}}+t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & ={{J}}-\frac{2Q}{{{B}}+t}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{2}{{{B}}+t}Q={{J}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.

This is a first-order linear equation with variable coefficients. So we find the general solution using an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(t) & ={e}^{\int 2/({{B}}+t)\,dt} \\  & ={e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡|{{B}}+t|} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡({{B}}+t)^{2}} \\  & =({{B}}+t)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the differential equation by $I(t)=({{B}}+t)^{2}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}({{B}}+t)^{2}\cdot (\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{2}{{{B}}+t}Q) & =({{B}}+t)^{2}\cdot {{J}} \\ ({{B}}+t)^{2}\frac{dQ}{dt}+2({{B}}+t)Q & ={{J}}({{B}}+t)^{2} \\ \frac{d}{dt}(Q({{B}}+t)^{2}) & ={{J}}({{B}}+t)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{d}{dt}(Q({{B}}+t)^{2})\,dt & =\int {{J}}({{B}}+t)^{2}\,dt \\ Q({{B}}+t)^{2} & ={{J}}\cdot \frac{1}{3}({{B}}+t)^{3}+C \\ Q(t) & ={{a}}({{B}}+t)+\frac{C}{({{B}}+t)^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $C$ is a constant of integration.

We're told that the tank initially contains ${{q0}}\,\text{kg}$ of preservative. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0)={{q0}},$ and solve for $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(0) & ={{q0}} \\ {{a}}({{B}}+0)+\frac{C}{({{B}}+0)^{2}} & ={{q0}} \\ {{alpha}}+\frac{C}{{{{B}}}^{2}} & ={{q0}} \\ \frac{C}{{{{B}}}^{2}} & =-{{deficit}} \\ C & =-{{deficit}}({{B}})^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(t) & ={{a}}({{B}}+t)-\frac{{{deficit}}({{B}})^{2}}{({{B}}+t)^{2}} \\  & ={{a}}({{B}}+t)-{{deficit}}{(\frac{{{B}}}{{{B}}+t})}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,  the amount of preservative in the tank ${{T}}$ minutes after pumping begins is

$$
\begin{aligned}Q({{T}}) & ={{a}}({{B}}+{{T}})-{{deficit}}{(\frac{{{B}}}{{{B}}+{{T}}})}^{2} \\  & ={{partT}}-{{deficit}}{(\frac{{{B}}}{{{BT}}})}^{2} \\  & ≈{{rounded}}\,\text{kg},\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to two decimal places.

Since $Q$ is the amount of nutrient in the vat, the *concentration* of the mixed solution at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{{{V}}+{{delta}}t}\,\text{kg/L}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed liquid leaves at a rate of ${{rout}}\,\text{L/min},$ *nutrient* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =({{rout}}\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{{{V}}+{{delta}}t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}}) \\  & =({{rout}}\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{{{V}}+{{delta}}t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\cancel{\text{L}}}) \\  & =\frac{{{rout}}Q}{{{V}}+{{delta}}t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{Q}{{{B}}+t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & ={{J}}-\frac{Q}{{{B}}+t}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{1}{{{B}}+t}Q={{J}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.

This is a first-order linear equation with variable coefficients. So we find the general solution using an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(t) & ={e}^{\int 1/({{B}}+t)\,dt} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡|{{B}}+t|} \\  & ={{B}}+t\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the differential equation by $I(t)={{B}}+t$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}({{B}}+t)\cdot (\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{1}{{{B}}+t}Q) & =({{B}}+t)\cdot {{J}} \\ ({{B}}+t)\frac{dQ}{dt}+Q & ={{J}}({{B}}+t) \\ \frac{d}{dt}(Q({{B}}+t)) & ={{J}}({{B}}+t).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{d}{dt}(Q({{B}}+t))\,dt & =\int {{J}}({{B}}+t)\,dt \\ Q({{B}}+t) & ={{J}}\cdot \frac{1}{2}({{B}}+t)^{2}+C \\ Q(t) & ={{a}}({{B}}+t)+\frac{C}{{{B}}+t}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $C$ is a constant of integration.

We're told that the vat initially contains ${{q0}}\,\text{kg}$ of nutrient. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0)={{q0}},$ and solve for $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(0) & ={{q0}} \\ {{a}}({{B}}+0)+\frac{C}{{{B}}+0} & ={{q0}} \\ {{alpha}}+\frac{C}{{{B}}} & ={{q0}} \\ \frac{C}{{{B}}} & =-{{deficit}} \\ C & =-{{absC}}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(t) & ={{a}}({{B}}+t)-\frac{{{absC}}}{{{B}}+t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,  the amount of nutrient in the vat ${{T}}$ minutes after pumping begins is

$$
\begin{aligned}Q({{T}}) & ={{a}}({{B}}+{{T}})-\frac{{{absC}}}{{{B}}+{{T}}} \\  & ={{partT}}-\frac{{{absC}}}{{{BT}}} \\  & ≈{{rounded}}\,\text{kg},\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to two decimal places.
